content:
The test image shows a corn ear/pod with dark black masses visible through torn, dried husks. The ear appears destroyed/replaced by dark material. This is a pod/ear issue.

Top candidates: Head_Smut, Common_Smut, Diplodia_Ear_Rot, Gibberella_Disease, Trichoderma_Ear_Rot.

Let me check references one at a time.
Head_Smut reference shows dark spore masses replacing the ear inside dried husks - very similar to test image. Let me check other candidates.
Common_Smut shows distinctive white/silvery bulbous galls - doesn't match the test image which shows complete ear replacement with dark mass. Let me check more candidates.
Diplodia_Ear_Rot shows ears with visible kernels and white mycelium - very different from the test image. Let me check more.
Gibberella shows pink/red mold on husks - very different. Let me check Trichoderma_Ear_Rot and other candidates.
Trichoderma shows green-gray mold on husks - different from test image. Let me check Aspergillus and Fusarium.
Aspergillus shows olive-green powdery mold on kernels - not a match. Let me check Fusarium.
Fusarium shows white/pink mold on individual kernels - not a match. Now let me view a second Head_Smut reference to confirm the match.

This second Head_Smut reference is an excellent match. It shows the same pattern as the test image: husks peeled back revealing a dark black mass of spores that has completely replaced the ear contents. The dried husks, dark spore mass inside, and overall ear appearance are very consistent.

The test image shows:
- Dark black spore mass replacing the ear interior
- Dried, torn husks surrounding the mass
- No visible kernels remaining
- Ear still attached to stalk

This matches Head_Smut perfectly: large smut galls replace ears, dark brown/black spore masses fill the husks, teardrop-shaped ears. This is distinct from Common_Smut (which shows round silvery-white galls) and all the ear rot diseases (which show mold on visible kernels).
